pages.title: A triple bond is a local structural feature

blocks.text: Ethyne is a small hydrocarbon with a C≡C bond. Compared with ethene, it has fewer hydrogens and a different geometry. The triple bond influences both addition reactions and the unusual acidity of a hydrogen directly attached to its carbon.

Alkynes contain a carbon–carbon triple bond. An open-chain hydrocarbon with one triple bond and no other unsaturation has formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. This formula is not sufficient to identify every unknown structure, because other combinations of rings or multiple bonds can have the same hydrogen count.

pages.transition: Naming tells us where the triple bond lies in the carbon chain.

pages.title: Name and locate the triple bond

blocks.text: Choose a suitable longest carbon chain containing C≡C, number to give it the lower locant in the simple examples, and use –yne. HC≡CH is ethyne; CH3C≡CH is propyne. The locant states where the triple bond starts in the numbered parent.
HC≡CCH2CH3 is but-1-yne, while CH3C≡CCH3 is but-2-yne. They are position isomers with formula C4H6. Pent-1-yne and 3-methylbut-1-yne illustrate different carbon skeletons with the same C5H8 formula.
An equivalent here is an amount relative to the amount of alkyne. One mole of H2 per mole alkyne removes one π bond; two moles are required to remove both π bonds in complete hydrogenation.

pages.transition: Its local orbital arrangement explains both linear geometry and bond count.

pages.title: One sigma bond and two pi bonds

blocks.text: Each triply bonded carbon is sp hybridised, giving two linear bond directions at 180°. The remaining two p orbitals form two π bonds by sideways overlap in perpendicular planes. The C≡C thus contains one σ and two π bonds.

For HC≡CH, the C–C connection contributes one σ and two π bonds. Two C–H connections add two σ bonds. Total: three σ and two π. The molecule is linear, not a bent structure suggested by drawing the triple lines as separate paths between atoms.

pages.transition: Calcium carbide provides a direct preparation of the smallest alkyne.

pages.title: Prepare ethyne from calcium carbide

blocks.text: CaC2 + 2H2O → HC≡CH + Ca(OH)2. One mole calcium carbide yields one mole ethyne in the ideal stoichiometric conversion. Calcium carbide can itself be made by heating calcium oxide with carbon: CaO + 3C → CaC2 + CO.

The carbon pair in carbide becomes the carbon pair in ethyne; water supplies hydrogen. Check the Ca, C and H balances separately in the respective equations. Calcium carbide’s reaction with water can be vigorous and generates flammable gas, requiring appropriate laboratory or industrial controls.

pages.transition: A dihalide offers another route through two successive eliminations.

pages.title: A two-stage elimination from a dihalide

blocks.text: A vicinal dihalide can lose HX in stages. Alcoholic KOH removes one HX to give an alkenyl halide; removal of the second HX from that stronger unsaturated arrangement requires a stronger base such as sodamide, NaNH2, in the elementary preparation described.

From 1,2-dibromoethane, one elimination gives bromoethene, CH2=CHBr. A second elimination gives ethyne, HC≡CH. Both H and Br are removed in each stage, and the carbon skeleton remains intact. Do not assume ordinary alcoholic KOH alone completes every double elimination efficiently.

pages.transition: The product’s physical behaviour still reflects its hydrocarbon character.

pages.title: Physical properties still resemble hydrocarbons

blocks.text: Alkynes have low water solubility and dissolve in suitable organic solvents. Their boiling points generally rise with increasing molecular size. The strong covalent triple bond acts within a molecule; it does not mean neighbouring alkyne molecules are joined into one ionic lattice.

The C≡C bond is shorter and stronger overall than C=C or C–C. Nonetheless its π electrons can take part in addition reactions. As with alkenes, distinguish total bond strength from the reactivity of an accessible π system towards a particular reagent.

pages.transition: The special chemical behaviour of a terminal hydrogen needs a separate explanation.

pages.title: The terminal hydrogen behaves differently

blocks.text: A terminal alkyne contains –C≡C–H, with H directly bonded to an sp carbon. An internal alkyne lacks that terminal H. Removing H⁺ from the terminal bond leaves a conjugate-base lone pair on sp carbon, whose high s character holds electrons relatively close to the nucleus.

This helps make terminal alkynes more acidic than comparable alkenes or alkanes, although they remain weak acids and need sufficiently strong bases. A hydrogen on a methyl group beside a triple bond is not the terminal alkyne hydrogen being discussed.

pages.transition: A strong base lets us express that acidity in a balanced reaction.

pages.title: Write acid–base reactions with correct charge

blocks.text: CH3C≡CH + NaNH2 → CH3C≡C⁻ Na⁺ + NH3. Sodamide removes the terminal proton and yields an acetylide salt. Atom and charge accounting shows that the carbon skeleton stays intact while H transfers to NH2⁻.

With sodium metal, the balanced single-deprotonation example is 2HC≡CH + 2Na → 2HC≡C⁻ Na⁺ + H2. Two terminal H atoms combine to form one H2; writing one ethyne plus one sodium with a whole H2 product would not conserve hydrogen.

pages.transition: The two π bonds also permit successive additions under suitable conditions.

pages.title: Addition uses the two pi bonds in stages

blocks.text: An alkyne can add one equivalent of a reagent across one π bond and then another across the remaining unsaturation. Complete hydrogenation consumes two H2 per triple bond and gives an alkane; suitably controlled partial hydrogenation can stop at the alkene.

But-2-yne cannot form a terminal acetylide merely because it contains a triple bond: it has no H attached directly to a triple-bonded carbon. The distinctions terminal/internal and one/two equivalents are necessary for predicting acidity and addition products accurately.

Teacher-created stoichiometry check: 0.0500 mol terminal alkyne requires 0.0500 mol NH2⁻ to remove one terminal proton per molecule, but complete hydrogenation of the same number of triple bonds requires 0.100 mol H2. Acidity and addition consume different reagents through different bond changes.

pages.transition: Let us distinguish terminal acidity from the additions possible at any triple bond.

pages.title: Use location, geometry and stoichiometry together

blocks.text: For one acyclic triple bond, use CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, locate –yne in the name and assign sp geometry at the two involved carbons. C≡C contains one σ and two π bonds; HC≡CH therefore contains three σ bonds in total.

Carbide hydrolysis and staged dihalide elimination provide preparation routes. Only terminal alkynes bear the special acidic C≡C–H discussed here. Strong-base deprotonation preserves the skeleton and produces an acetylide, while complete hydrogenation needs two H2 per triple bond.

questions.question: Which of but-1-yne and but-2-yne has an acidic terminal alkyne H?
questions.answer: But-1-yne, HC≡CCH2CH3. But-2-yne has carbon groups at both ends of C≡C.

questions.question: How many σ and π bonds are in ethyne?
questions.answer: Three σ bonds: one C–C and two C–H; two π bonds in C≡C.

questions.question: Why is sodamide needed after the first elimination from a vicinal dihalide?
questions.answer: The remaining alkenyl halide requires stronger conditions to eliminate the second HX and create the triple bond.

questions.question: Why is terminal alkyne acidity greater than alkane acidity?
questions.answer: The conjugate-base pair is held in an sp orbital with higher s character, stabilising it relative to the corresponding less s-rich carbon orbitals.

questions.question: Correct HC≡CH + Na → HC≡CNa + H2.
questions.answer: 2HC≡CH + 2Na → 2HC≡CNa + H2. Two removed H atoms produce one H2 molecule.
